Evaluation Has David done evaluation work on AI systems?
Yes — the chatbot you're talking to is the example I'd point at. I built a retrieval evaluation suite for it: a golden set of labelled questions split into development and held-out portions, five retrieval configurations scored against identical labels, and a CI gate that fails the build if retrieval quality regresses. The results are published on the portfolio project page, including the ones that were unflattering. The evaluation is also what chose the configuration that ships.

ing the ones that were unflattering. The evaluation is also what chose the configuration that ships. How does David evaluate a RAG system?
I start by deciding what "good" means before measuring anything. For retrieval I label a set of realistic questions with the phrases a correct answer has to be grounded in, then score configurations on hit rate, recall, MRR, and nDCG. I gate CI on hit@k specifically, because that's what determines whether the model can answer at all — the other metrics are informative but make poor gates. I set thresholds below measured performance as regression floors, never as targets, because tuning until a threshold is cleared is just fitting to your own test set. I also hold back a portion of the labelled questions and never look at them while making a decision, so the numbers I publish aren't the numbers something was tuned against.

em while making a decision, so the numbers I publish aren't the numbers something was tuned against. Why does David label relevance by phrase instead of by document?
Because the corpus gets re-split every time a source document changes. Labels tied to a chunk's identity are invalidated on every rebuild, so they rot faster than you can maintain them. Phrases survive re-chunking, which is what makes the labelled set an asset instead of a chore.

them. Phrases survive re-chunking, which is what makes the labelled set an asset instead of a chore. What has David's evaluation work actually found?
Two real bugs that no test caught, and one wrong architecture. A tokenizer mismatch between index-time and query-time was silently destroying keyword recall — fixing it moved MRR from 0.745 to 0.892. A rank-fusion constant taken from a paper was being used at the wrong scale, which meant one of the two retrievers could never contribute a result; fusion was running, passing its tests, and doing nothing. In both of those cases every component behaved exactly as specified and only a metric moved. The third finding was bigger: the hybrid semantic-plus-keyword pipeline with a cross-encoder lost to plain keyword search on every metric, so I deleted it rather than tuned it.

a cross-encoder lost to plain keyword search on every metric, so I deleted it rather than tuned it. Does David use evaluation results to change what he builds? That's the entire point of collecting them. The eval showed that plain keyword search was beating my hybrid pipeline with a cross-encoder on every metric, which is not the result I wanted after building it. Rather than quietly retuning a fusion weight to make the number look better, I added a configuration that asked the actual question — keyword results fed straight to the cross-encoder, with no semantic search at all — and it beat the full pipeline. Then the cross-encoder failed the same test against keyword search alone. So the fix was to delete architecture rather than add it: production now runs keyword search only, which cut the backend from 87 production dependencies to 40 and the deployed container image from 17.2GB to 544MB — most of that being the CUDA libraries that torch pulls in behind the embedding model, shipped into a container with no GPU.

CUDA libraries that torch pulls in behind the embedding model, shipped into a container with no GPU. I keep an append-only findings log on the project page recording what each measurement showed and what changed in the code because of it.

the project page recording what each measurement showed and what changed in the code because of it. Why doesn't David's chatbot use semantic or vector search?
It did, and the evaluation said it wasn't earning its place on this corpus. Retrieval is BM25 keyword search over a stemmed, stopword-filtered index. I'm not claiming semantic search is a bad idea in general — this corpus is written as anticipated questions and answers, which is exactly the condition that flatters keyword matching, and I expect that to stop being true as the corpus grows. The semantic and re-ranking configurations are still implemented and still measured on every evaluation run, so when the answer flips it'll be a measurement that tells me, not a rebuild.

every evaluation run, so when the answer flips it'll be a measurement that tells me, not a rebuild. How does David keep published metrics from going stale?
The numbers aren't written by hand anywhere. CI runs the evaluation, writes the results to a file, and commits it; the project page and the repository docs both render from that file. Even the sentence comparing the shipped configuration to the best-scoring one is generated from the data, so the write-up can't drift into claiming something the measurements no longer support.

What has David not measured yet?
Retrieval quality is only half of a RAG system's behaviour. Generation faithfulness — does the answer stay inside the retrieved context? — plus refusal behaviour on out-of-scope questions and adversarial robustness are all still unmeasured. I'd rather name those gaps than imply the evaluation covers more than it does.

Overview

Generate Music with AI is a full-stack web application that turns a text prompt into an original music track using ACE-Step, a text-to-music generation model, running on serverless GPUs. You describe the vibe — _"lo-fi hip hop with rain ambiance"_ or _"aggressive metalcore with a jazz breakdown"_ — and the app composes something that didn't exist a moment before.

The project started as an experiment to close the loop between natural language and audio generation. Rather than wrapping a simple API call in a form, I wanted to build the full production-quality system: input validation, rate limiting, async job polling, streaming audio playback, and a UI that responds gracefully to the latency inherent in GPU inference.

How It Works

The user fills out a prompt form on the Next.js frontend and submits. From there, every layer has a specific job:

s out a prompt form on the Next.js frontend and submits. From there, every layer has a specific job: 1. FastAPI backend (Railway) receives the request, validates input, checks rate limits using  with session-cookie keying, then proxies the payload to the ACE-Step API running on Modal.
2. Modal spins up a GPU worker, runs the ACE-Step model, and returns a  immediately — the job is asynchronous.
3. Frontend polls  at an interval until the job completes, showing a live progress indicator.
4. Audio delivery: once complete, the frontend fetches the audio stream from  and renders it in a WaveSurfer.js waveform player.

The backend is a stateless proxy — no audio data is stored server-side. Every request is forwarded to Modal and the response is passed back. This keeps the Railway deployment lightweight and cheap.

Technical Architecture

The architecture is deliberately layered to separate concerns cleanly:

Key engineering decisions:

The architecture is deliberately layered to separate concerns cleanly:

Key engineering decisions: - HTTP/2 with httpx: The  is instantiated once at startup via FastAPI's lifespan context and shared across all requests. This avoids TCP handshake overhead on every generation request and enables multiplexed connections to Modal.
- Session-based rate limiting: Rate limits key on the session cookie and fall back to IP, which prevents one user from exhausting another's quota while handling clients behind shared NAT correctly.
- Typed API client: The Next.js frontend uses a hand-rolled typed fetch wrapper with Zod validation for all API responses. API errors surface as  instances with structured context rather than raw exceptions.
- Job polling over WebSockets: Modal's ACE-Step API uses a job queue model. Polling was simpler to implement correctly and debug than maintaining a persistent WebSocket connection through a serverless reverse proxy.

Skills Demonstrated

intaining a persistent WebSocket connection through a serverless reverse proxy.

Skills Demonstrated This project touches every layer of a modern AI-integrated web application — from GPU inference orchestration down to waveform rendering. The engineering decisions were practical ones: stateless proxy to minimize Railway costs, shared HTTP client to reduce latency, typed API contract to catch integration bugs early. Building this sharpened my ability to design systems that are observable, cost-conscious, and handle async complexity without leaking it to the user.

Overview

Baby Names Explorer is an interactive data application for exploring 145 years of US baby name trends from the Social Security Administration. You can browse the most popular names for any year since 1880, pull up the full history of any single name with a statistical forecast of where it's heading, and ask questions about the whole dataset in plain English.

The project grew from a simple question: _is a name getting more or less popular, and will that trend continue?_ The SSA publishes name data going back to 1880, but raw data files are not interactive. Building this meant designing a data pipeline, working out a forecasting approach that holds up under validation, and wrapping it in a UI that makes the analysis accessible.

It started as a single-file Streamlit app. It has since been rebuilt as a Next.js frontend over a FastAPI backend, with the querying, forecasting, and chatbot logic split into services that can be tested independently of the UI.

Data Pipeline

ng, and chatbot logic split into services that can be tested independently of the UI.

Data Pipeline The SSA doesn't offer a direct API download — the data comes as a ZIP archive from a page that blocks automated requests. The pipeline handles this with Selenium to automate the download, then processes all ~145 annual text files into a single normalized dataset.

For each name-sex-year combination, the pipeline computes:

-  — raw number of births with that name
-  — count as a fraction of all births that year and sex, correcting for population growth
-  — ranking within year and sex (1 = most popular)

t year and sex, correcting for population growth
-  — ranking within year and sex (1 = most popular) Relative metrics matter more than raw counts here. A mid-century name given to 30,000 babies was a genuine cultural phenomenon; the same raw count today, spread across a far larger and far more varied pool of births, is not. Share of births says which of those two happened. The pipeline also back-fills zero-count rows so every name has a continuous yearly series rather than gaps, which matters downstream — a time-series model can't be fit to a series with holes in it. The result is stored in a SQLite database the backend queries read-only.

Forecasting

The forecasting task is time-series prediction: given a name's popularity trajectory, project where it goes over the next five years. The approach is ARIMA, and most of the work is in choosing the model rather than running it.

For each name, the backend:

, and most of the work is in choosing the model rather than running it.

For each name, the backend: 1. Log-transforms series with high relative variance, since name popularity tends to grow and decay multiplicatively rather than by fixed increments.
2. Determines the differencing order by running ADF and KPSS stationarity tests and differencing until both agree the series is stationary.
3. Grid-searches ARIMA orders around that differencing order, selecting by AICc — the small-sample-corrected criterion, which matters because some names only have a few decades of usable history.
4. Validates on a five-year holdout: refit on everything but the last five years, forecast forward, and report MAE, RMSE, and MAPE against what actually happened.
5. Runs residual diagnostics — Ljung-Box for autocorrelation, Jarque-Bera for normality, ARCH for heteroscedasticity — and surfaces whether the fit actually satisfies the model's assumptions.

CH for heteroscedasticity — and surfaces whether the fit actually satisfies the model's assumptions. Forecasts are returned with 80% and 95% confidence intervals rather than a single line. A single point forecast implies a precision this data doesn't support, and the interval width is the honest way to say so. Fitting is CPU-bound, so results are cached per name and sex.

Natural-Language Querying

Diamonds: Predicting Price is a regression analysis project that models diamond prices from physical and quality attributes, written end to end in R. The analysis covers a dataset of ~54,000 diamonds with features including carat weight, cut grade, color grade, clarity grade, and physical dimensions (length, width, depth).

This was my earliest end-to-end data science project. I'm including it here not as a showcase of technical sophistication, but as evidence of where I started — and because the analytical thinking it required is genuinely interesting.

The Analysis The central challenge is that diamond price is not linear in any single feature. Carat weight has the strongest correlation with price, but two diamonds with the same carat weight can differ in price by an order of magnitude based on cut, color, and clarity. These quality grades interact with each other and with size in complex ways.

The analysis proceeded in several phases:

Exploratory data analysis: Distribution analysis revealed that carat weight clusters at round values (0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5) due to market conventions, and that price distributions are right-skewed. The EDA also surfaced a data quality problem worth handling before modeling: a small number of diamonds have a recorded length, width, or depth of exactly zero, which is physically impossible. Those were converted to NAs rather than silently left in as valid measurements.

ysically impossible. Those were converted to NAs rather than silently left in as valid measurements. Feature ordering: The raw quality grades (cut: Fair → Ideal, color: J → D, clarity: I1 → IF) are ordinal categories, and color ships in an order that runs best-to-worst while the others run worst-to-best. Reordering it to match makes the model coefficients read consistently across all three grades instead of one of them pointing the opposite way.

Modeling: The analysis works through four families on an 80/20 train-test split — simple and multivariate linear regression, regression decision trees (with complexity-parameter tuning), random forests, and gradient boosting machines — fitting each against both the 4 C's alone and the full feature set, and scoring every one by MAE, RMSE, and adjusted R² on the held-out data. Linear regression is the interpretable baseline; the ensembles capture the non-linear interactions more accurately at the cost of interpretability. A final comparison table ranks all of them side by side.

What I Learned The most important thing this project taught me wasn't a modeling technique — it was that fitting the model is the small part. Most of the work was upstream of it: deciding what a zero-length diamond means, getting the ordinal grades into a consistent order, and choosing which features a given model should even see. By the time the data was right, swapping between a linear model and a random forest was a few lines. That ratio has held on every project since.

ween a linear model and a random forest was a few lines. That ratio has held on every project since. It also gave me an early appreciation for confounding. Plot price against cut on its own and the trend is missing — _Ideal_ diamonds don't command an obvious premium over _Fair_ ones, which is the opposite of what the grade is supposed to mean. The explanation isn't gemological, it's compositional: buyers chasing large stones tend to trade away cut quality, so the poorly cut diamonds in the data are also the biggest ones, and carat swamps the effect being measured. Any single feature plotted against price in this dataset is really showing you carat until you control for it.

Overview

Chat with Nietzsche is a conversational AI that channels Friedrich Nietzsche's philosophical voice using Retrieval-Augmented Generation over his complete written works. You can ask it about the Will to Power, Eternal Recurrence, master-slave morality, or why it thinks modern social media would have disgusted him — and get answers grounded in Nietzsche's actual writings, with source citations to the passages used.

The goal was never to make a philosophical trivia bot. It was to build a system where responses are _demonstrably_ faithful to the source material. Every answer the system produces can be traced back to real text from the 19 works in the corpus.

It began as a single-file Streamlit app. It has since been rebuilt as a full-stack application — a Next.js frontend talking to a FastAPI backend that owns the retrieval pipeline and streams tokens back to the browser.

The RAG Pipeline

The RAG Pipeline The retrieval pipeline is multi-stage, designed to maximize the quality of context passed to the LLM rather than relying on the model alone.

esigned to maximize the quality of context passed to the LLM rather than relying on the model alone. 1. Question condensing: When there's conversation history, one LLM call rewrites the follow-up into a standalone question. _"What did he mean by that?"_ becomes something a search index can actually answer. The rewrite is used for retrieval only — the original message is what the model responds to. 2. Hybrid search: The condensed query hits both a FAISS semantic index (70% weight) and a BM25 keyword index (30% weight) over roughly 7,300 chunks. Semantic search handles conceptual overlap; BM25 ensures exact philosophical terms like _"Ressentiment"_ or _"Zarathustra"_ are matched precisely. 3. Fragment filtering: Candidate passages shorter than two sentences are dropped. Chunking at paragraph boundaries occasionally yields a stray heading or one-line aphorism fragment, and those crowd out passages that carry an actual argument. 4. Cross-encoder re-ranking: The survivors are re-ranked using , a cross-encoder that scores each passage against the question jointly rather than independently.

g , a cross-encoder that scores each passage against the question jointly rather than independently. This separates genuinely relevant passages from those that merely share vocabulary. The top 6 make it through. 5. Grounded generation: Those passages, the persona prompt, and the last 10 turns of history go to Groq. Temperature is set to 0.3 — low enough to suppress creative invention, high enough to avoid robotic phrasing — and tokens stream straight to the browser as they're produced.

gh enough to avoid robotic phrasing — and tokens stream straight to the browser as they're produced. Technical Implementation

Corpus and chunking: All 19 works were sourced from Project Gutenberg public domain translations. Text is split at paragraph boundaries with a 1200-character target and 150-character overlap. Paragraph-based chunking preserves argumentative flow — Nietzsche's writing often builds meaning across a full paragraph, and mid-sentence splits would corrupt the context.

Embeddings:  generates 768-dimensional dense vectors for each chunk. The same model embeds user queries at inference time, ensuring semantic alignment between document and query spaces.

mbeds user queries at inference time, ensuring semantic alignment between document and query spaces. Stack: FastAPI serves the retrieval pipeline and the streaming chat endpoint. FAISS and BM25 (rank-bm25) are driven directly rather than through an orchestration framework — the pipeline is specific enough that a framework's abstractions cost more than they save. Indexes are built offline and committed to the repo, so a cold start never re-embeds the corpus. The Next.js frontend never talks to the backend directly: a server-side route validates each request and proxies it, piping the token stream through unchanged.

Source citations: The UI surfaces the specific Nietzsche passages used to generate each response — title, translator, and a link to the Gutenberg source — alongside the answer. This transparency serves two purposes: it lets users verify authenticity, and it demonstrates that the retrieval pipeline found genuinely relevant context rather than hallucinating.

demonstrates that the retrieval pipeline found genuinely relevant context rather than hallucinating. Deployment: The frontend runs on Vercel; the backend runs on Railway from a Docker image with the embedding and cross-encoder models baked in, so cold starts never wait on a model download. It's the same split used by the AI music generator, and the reasoning is the same: the CPU-and-memory-hungry half gets a container it can size independently of the UI.

Skills Demonstrated

This project required implementing every component of an advanced RAG pipeline from first principles — no managed vector database, no off-the-shelf retrieval API. The multi-stage retrieve-filter-rerank design reflects real production RAG patterns used in enterprise retrieval systems. Rebuilding it from a Streamlit prototype into a streaming full-stack app forced the harder questions a demo never asks: what the API contract between the halves should be, where conversation state lives, and how to keep a cold start from timing out a user's first question.

Overview

This is the site you are reading. It is also the project I would point at first in a technical interview, because it is the one where I can show you numbers instead of adjectives.

The visible half is a Next.js front end. The interesting half is the chatbot in the corner: a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that answers questions about my experience from my own resume and a written Q&A corpus, streaming responses through a FastAPI backend. Plenty of portfolios have a chatbot bolted on. What I wanted was the thing most of them skip — a way to know whether the retrieval underneath it actually works, and a gate that fails the build when it stops working.

The problem with "it seems to work"

The problem with "it seems to work" A RAG pipeline gives you a lot of knobs and very little feedback. Mine started with the parameters you would expect: a weighted blend of semantic and keyword search, ten candidates narrowed to five by a second model. Every one of those numbers was a guess. I had no answer to _"does the re-ranking stage earn its latency?"_ or _"would keyword search alone be just as good?"_, and nothing would have told me if a change to how documents get split quietly broke retrieval.

That is the situation evaluation exists for, and it is not specific to this project. Any system whose output is text has the same problem: it is always producing something plausible, so "it seems to work" is the default state whether it works or not. The only way out is to decide in advance what good means, label enough ground truth to measure it, and put the measurement somewhere it can fail.

How I decided what "good" means

truth to measure it, and put the measurement somewhere it can fail.

How I decided what "good" means The golden set is a set of questions of the kind a recruiter, hiring manager, or technical interviewer actually asks — employment history, specific technologies, project details, education, logistics. Each one is labelled with the phrases a correct answer has to be grounded in.

Labelling by _phrase_ rather than by document ID is the decision I would defend hardest. The corpus gets re-split every time I edit a source document, so any label tied to a chunk's identity is invalidated on every rebuild — the labels would rot faster than I could maintain them. Phrases survive re-chunking, which is what makes the golden set an asset rather than a chore.

The metrics are chosen for what they decide, not for what is easy to report: - hit@5 — did _any_ relevant passage reach the model? This is the one that gates the build, because it is what determines whether the system can answer at all.
- recall@5 — what share of the relevant passages made it. Reported, deliberately not gated: several questions have more than five relevant passages, so their recall is capped below 1.0 by construction and no honest threshold could ever be met. A metric you cannot set a fair threshold on is a metric you should not gate on.
- MRR and nDCG@5 — how far up the list the good passage landed, which matters because a model attends unevenly across a long context.

The thresholds sit _below_ measured performance with headroom for noise. They are floors, not targets. Tuning parameters until a floor is cleared would be fitting to my own test set, which produces numbers that look better and mean less.

The questions are split into a development portion and a held-out portion, and the table below reports the held-out one. Choices about the architecture are made against the development questions; the held-out questions are never looked at while making one. It is a smaller sample and therefore a coarser number, and I would rather publish a coarse number that means what it says than a precise one that is really the score of whatever configuration won on the questions used to pick it. The split is assigned by hashing each question's ID, so I cannot move an inconvenient question across the line without it showing up in a test.

What the evaluation changed

Metrics are only worth collecting if they alter what you build. This is the running record of what the harness found and what I did about it — appended to, never rewritten.

Two of those entries share a pattern I found useful to learn: the code looked correct, every component behaved exactly as specified, every test passed, and nothing was going to surface the problem except a number moving. Unit tests tell you the parts do what you said; only measurement tells you the system does what you meant.

ests tell you the parts do what you said; only measurement tells you the system does what you meant. The third one is the one I would actually want to be asked about. I built a hybrid retrieval pipeline — semantic search fused with keyword search, then a cross-encoder re-ranking the candidates — because that is the architecture you build when you are demonstrating that you can build it. The evaluation said plain keyword search beat it on every metric. The tempting response was to retune the fusion weights until the numbers came back, and that would have been the wrong experiment: under the fusion formula I was using, tuning the semantic weight toward zero and switching the semantic stage off are the same experiment, so "find the optimal ratio" would have been a slower path to the answer I already had, ending in a magic constant with nothing behind it. So I ran the experiment that actually asked the question — keyword candidates fed straight to the re-ranker, no semantic stage at all — and it beat the full pipeline. Then the re-ranker failed the same test against keyword search alone.

and it beat the full pipeline. Then the re-ranker failed the same test against keyword search alone. The fix was to delete the architecture. Production retrieval is now keyword search and nothing else, which cut the backend from 87 production dependencies to 40 and the deployed container image from 17.2GB to 544MB. Most of that was not the model weights — it was , which the embedding library pulls in, and whose default Linux wheels ship the NVIDIA CUDA runtime into a container that has no GPU. I had been deploying several gigabytes of GPU libraries to serve keyword search, and nothing was ever going to tell me that except deciding the stage that needed them had not earned its place. Cheaper _and_ better is a stronger result than a tuned constant, and it is not the result I wanted when I started. Every deleted stage is still measured as a configuration on every run, because this corpus is written as anticipated questions and answers — the exact condition that flatters keyword matching — and I expect that to stop being true as the corpus grows.

The eval is a CI gate, not a notebook. It runs on every backend change and fails the build if the shipped configuration drops below its floor, so retrieval quality cannot regress silently between commits. The other configurations are measured and published for comparison but not gated: a floor exists to stop a change degrading what a visitor is served, and nothing is served by a configuration production does not run. Because production is now keyword-only, the gate itself runs in seconds and needs no model weights at all.

My resume is a source document for the index, and it carried my home address and phone number, which meant the chatbot would read them back to anyone who asked. The fix was three-layered: strip it at the source, redact it during the index build as a backstop, and add a regression test that fails the build if a phone number or street address ever appears in the committed index again. The redaction and the detection are deliberately asymmetric — the redactor is precise, because rewriting the corpus silently means a false positive destroys real content unnoticed, while the test guard casts a wide net, because its only power is to fail a build and a false positive there costs one glance from me.

What I am not claiming The corpus is small, and much of it is written as anticipated questions with answers — which is exactly the condition that favours keyword matching over semantic search. Relevance is also labelled by exact phrase presence, which is close to what keyword ranking measures. Every configuration is scored against identical labels, so the comparison is internally fair, but any conclusion it supports is about _this_ corpus rather than about retrieval in general.

That bias cuts directly against the conclusion I drew from it, which is why the retired configurations are still measured rather than deleted from the harness: the result that told me to remove them is the same result I expect to reverse as the corpus grows past the point where the questions and the documents share vocabulary.
